summary: Specifies community requirements for choosing venues for IETF plenary meetings, including hotels and meeting space, and tells the IASA to make additional process documents available describing how meeting selection currently works.

eli5.summary: This lists what a good place for a big IETF meeting must have, like rules for choosing a school trip location.

questions: how does ietf choose meeting locations
what are the ietf meeting venue requirements
what is an ietf overflow hotel
subtitle: The community's requirements for choosing where the IETF holds its plenary meetings, from mandatory facilities to nice-to-haves.

tldr.problem: The IETF needs a clear, shared statement of what a plenary meeting venue must offer, so the body that arranges meetings can be guided and held to the community's expectations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states core values and non-objectives, then sorts venue criteria into mandatory, important and other considerations. It requires the IASA to publicly document the roles and selection processes used.
tldr.outcome: The IASA has community guidance for choosing regions, cities, facilities and hotels. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 9712.

facts.value: One-third or more of projected attendees

sections.title: Purpose and Terms
sections.content:
The IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA, see RFC 8711) is responsible for arranging the selection and operation of the plenary meeting venue. This document guides the IASA in choosing regions, cities, facilities and hotels, with general criteria plus requirements for transparency and community consultation. The IASA still applies its own best judgment.

The RFC fixes four terms. A Venue is the city, meeting resources and guest room resources. The Facility is the building with the meeting rooms. IETF Hotels are hotels close to the Facility where room blocks are negotiated and IASA-managed network services are in use. Overflow Hotels have a negotiated group rate but are not usually connected to the IETF network.
sections.eli5: The group that organizes the meetings gets a guide to follow. It names the pieces: the city, the main building, the main hotels and the extra hotels.

sections.title: Core Values and Non-objectives
sections.content:
Several values run through the selection: meeting to pursue the IETF mission (RFC 3935), inclusiveness, meeting in different global locations to spread travel burden (policy in RFC 8719), unfiltered Internet access, focused technical discussion, economics, and least astonishment and openness.

On inclusiveness, the IETF seeks to minimize onerous entry regulations, or to rotate them so they do not always hit the same attendees, and to avoid countries with laws that effectively exclude people on the basis of race, ethnicity, religion, gender, sexual orientation, national origin, citizenship, or gender identity. Internet access means all forms of communication are allowed, including encrypted VPNs to corporate networks.

Venues are explicitly not chosen or declined to endorse or condemn countries, political paradigms, laws or policies. Maximal attendance is not a goal in itself, and neither is variety in site-seeing.
sections.eli5: The IETF wants a meeting place where anyone can come, the Internet works freely, people can talk without noise, and it does not cost too much. It is not picking places to make a political point or for sightseeing.

sections.title: Mandatory Criteria
sections.content:
If a mandatory criterion cannot be met, the location is unacceptable and the IASA MUST NOT enter into a contract. If the IASA learns after contracting that a location can no longer meet one, it informs the community and handles the matter case by case.

The Facility MUST have enough space in an appropriate layout for the expected participants, leadership and staff. The Facility and IETF Hotels MUST provide wheelchair access for the number of people expected to need it. And it MUST be possible to provision Internet access that lets in-person attendees use the Internet for all their needs, with enough bandwidth for remote attendees. This includes native and unmodified IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity and global reachability, and it MUST be possible to provision redundant paths.
sections.eli5: There are three things a place absolutely must have: enough room for everyone, wheelchair access, and good Internet. If it cannot do those, the IETF does not sign a deal.

sections.title: Important Criteria and Other Considerations
sections.content:
Important criteria are not mandatory but are highly significant, and may be traded off against each other across meetings. A venue meeting more of them is preferable. If one cannot be met but the venue is selected anyway, the IASA MUST notify the community at the announcement. They cover the city (acceptable travel cost and time, a likely host and sponsors, acceptable visa and travel barriers, acceptable economic, safety and health risks), the venue (written assurance of compliance with local health, safety and accessibility laws, places for ad hoc conversations within walking distance of 5-10 minutes, affordable costs, disability access), technical needs, hotels, and food and beverage.

For hotels, the IETF Hotels should be close to each other and the Facility, with guest rooms sufficient to house one-third or more of projected attendees. Overflow Hotels should be contractable at a variety of rates, and budget hotels should be nearby. At least one hotel or the Facility should have a lounge and a working space. Dietary needs, including health-related and religion-related ones, should be satisfiable on-site or through nearby groceries.

Other considerations are desirable but must not be traded off against the above: a preference for "One Roof", unfiltered Internet at Overflow Hotels, multi-event contracts, and a site-visit participant who knows both the locale and the IETF when a city is considered for the first time.
sections.eli5: Next come things that are very good to have, like close hotels, cheap food and easy travel. If a place misses one, the organizers must tell everyone. Then come bonuses that never outrank those.

sections.title: Documentation, Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC does not specify the selection process or who is responsible for meeting requirements. It does require that the IASA SHALL publicly document and keep current both a list of roles and responsibilities for IETF meetings and the selection processes used to fulfill the community's requirements.

The IANA Considerations section says there are no IANA actions. The Security Considerations say the note proposes no protocols and so introduces no new protocol insecurities. For privacy, different places have different constraints, so the IASA SHALL inform the IETF of privacy limitations it learns about when meetings are announced, for example regulatory authentication or logging requirements.
sections.eli5: The organizers have to write down who does what and how places get chosen, and keep it current. They must also warn people if a place has odd privacy rules.

items.title: Mandatory
items.text: Cannot be traded away. The IASA MUST NOT contract if one fails.

items.title: Important
items.text: Highly significant and can be balanced across meetings. The community must be told if one is not met.

items.title: Other considerations
items.text: Desirable, but not to be traded off against the more important criteria.
